meta.title: Who really said "Measure what is measurable, and make measurable what is not so"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Galileo — Thomas-Henri Martin, summarising his method in French in 1868. The line is a historian’s paraphrase that hardened into a quotation.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Measure what is measurable, and make measurable what is not so'?
meta.ogDescription: The sentence appears in no work of Galileo’s. Its earliest form is Th.-Henri Martin’s 1868 Galilée, p. 289 — written in indirect speech, not quoted.

answer.label: Not Galileo — Thomas-Henri Martin, describing him in 1868
answer.authorDates: 1813–1884 · French Hellenist, historian of science and dean of the Faculty of Letters at Rennes
answer.sourceLine: Wikiquote files the line among Galileo’s misattributed quotations ↗ and traces it, following Andreas Kleinert’s 2009 article in NTM, to two nineteenth-century French scholars. We read both books. The full two-part sentence first appears in Th.-Henri Martin’s Galilée (Paris: Didier, 1868), p. 289 ↗ — and not as a quotation: Martin writes “Il déclare que dans tous ces phénomènes il faut mesurer tout ce qui est mesurable, et tâcher de rendre mesurable tout ce qui ne l’est pas directement,” in indirect speech, in roman type, with no quotation marks anywhere near it. It is a historian’s summary of Galileo’s method that later readers promoted into Galileo’s own words.

source.heading: A summary that turned into a quotation

docMeta.dd: Galilée : les droits de la science et la méthode des sciences physiques
Indirect speech — Martin’s own sentence about Galileo, not a quotation of him

source.excerpt: … il sait que les phénomènes purement physiques doivent se réduire à des mouvements, les uns perceptibles pour nos sens, les autres imperceptibles pour nous à titre de mouvements appréciables. Il déclare que dans tous ces phénomènes il faut mesurer tout ce qui est mesurable, et tâcher de rendre mesurable tout ce qui ne l’est pas directement. Il ne s’agit donc pas de poser des principes, les uns métaphysiques, les autres mathématiques, puis d’essayer d’en conclure a priori quelles doivent être les lois physiques…
trail: English Wikiquote lists the line under Galileo’s misattributed quotations ↗ and names Antoine-Augustin Cournot and Thomas-Henri Martin as the real source, citing Andreas Kleinert, “Der messende Luchs: Zwei verbreitete Fehler in der Galilei-Literatur,” NTM Zeitschrift für Geschichte der Wissenschaften, Technik und Medizin 17, no. 2 (May 2009): 199–206.

German Wikiquote gives Kleinert’s finding in more detail ↗: there is no evidence for the sentence in Galileo’s writings; the earliest occurrence is Martin’s of 1868, with a shorter precursor in Cournot of 1847; and it was taken up and spread by Wilhelm Dilthey and Hermann Weyl. Kleinert’s article itself is behind a paywall we could not reach, so that chain of transmission rests on Wikiquote’s summary of it, not on our own reading.

We read Martin’s page rather than the summary of it. Page 289 of the 1868 scan ↗ carries the sentence in indirect speech — “Il déclare que…” — unquoted, in a paragraph reconstructing how Galileo thought about measurement.

And we read Cournot’s. De l’origine et des limites de la correspondance entre l’algèbre et la géométrie (Paris: L. Hachette, 1847), p. 375 ↗ has only the first half: true physics was founded, Cournot writes, the day Galileo conceived the idea of assigning to experiments “pour objet immédiat la mesure de tout ce qui peut être mesurable dans les phénomènes naturels.” The famous second clause — making measurable what is not — is not there.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the 1868 scan. The three words that matter are the first three: Il déclare que — “He declares that.” Everything after them is Martin’s prose about Galileo, in his own French, and it is set in ordinary roman type without a single quotation mark. In English the sentence reads roughly: he declares that in all these phenomena one must measure everything that is measurable, and try to make measurable everything that is not directly so.

sourceLink.text: Martin, Galilée (1868), p. 289, at the Internet Archive

source.rightsNote: Both documented sources are long out of copyright: Cournot’s book of 1847 ↗ and Martin’s of 1868 ↗ are freely readable at the Internet Archive. The English sentence at the top of this page is a different matter — it is an anonymous rendering of Martin’s French by a translator nobody has identified, of a date nobody has established, so we assert no rights status for it rather than guess one.

author.name: Thomas-Henri Martin
author.heading: About Thomas-Henri Martin
author.metaLine: 1813–1884 · French Hellenist, historian of science and philosopher
author.bio: Thomas-Henri Martin was born at Bellême in 1813, entered the École normale in 1831, and took his doctorate in 1836 with a Latin thesis on Spinoza. He spent his career at Rennes, as professor of ancient literature and eventually dean of the Faculty of Letters, and made his name on the boundary between classical scholarship and the history of science — a long edition of and commentary on Plato’s Timaeus, studies of ancient astronomy, and in 1868 Galilée : les droits de la science et la méthode des sciences physiques. He died at Rennes in 1884, and the one sentence of his that everybody knows is filed under somebody else’s name.

cite.sourceCitation: Th.-Henri Martin, Galilée : les droits de la science et la méthode des sciences physiques (Paris: Didier, 1868), 289: “Il déclare que dans tous ces phénomènes il faut mesurer tout ce qui est mesurable, et tâcher de rendre mesurable tout ce qui ne l’est pas directement.” Written in indirect speech, unquoted. Earlier half-form in Antoine-Augustin Cournot, De l’origine et des limites de la correspondance entre l’algèbre et la géométrie (Paris: L. Hachette, 1847), 375.

copyAttribution: "Measure what is measurable, and make measurable what is not so." — Not Galileo. The sentence is Th.-Henri Martin's, written about Galileo in indirect speech and never in quotation marks: "Il déclare que dans tous ces phénomènes il faut mesurer tout ce qui est mesurable, et tâcher de rendre mesurable tout ce qui ne l'est pas directement," Galilée : les droits de la science et la méthode des sciences physiques (Paris: Didier, 1868), p. 289. A shorter form, without the second clause, is in Cournot, De l'origine et des limites de la correspondance entre l'algèbre et la géométrie (Paris: L. Hachette, 1847), p. 375. Traced by Quotle.info.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is the tidiest one-line statement of the experimental method anyone has written, which is why it has been handed to the man who invented the method. He did not write it.

items.why: The sentence occurs nowhere in his works. English Wikiquote files it under “Misattributed” ↗ and German Wikiquote states flatly that there is no evidence for it in his writings ↗, both citing Kleinert’s 2009 study.

items.scope: The actual source of the full sentence
items.why: Read from the scan ↗: Martin writes it as his own summary, in indirect speech, without quotation marks. He is describing what Galileo declares, in the way any historian describes a subject’s position — and the sentence was later lifted out of his paragraph and put between quotation marks.

On p. 375 of his 1847 book ↗ Cournot credits Galileo with making experiments aim at “the measurement of everything that can be measurable in natural phenomena.” That is the first clause and only the first clause; the paradoxical half that makes the line quotable is Martin’s addition twenty-one years later.

German Wikiquote, summarising Kleinert, says the line was taken up and circulated by Dilthey and Weyl ↗. We could not read Kleinert’s article ourselves — it sits behind a publisher paywall this build could not reach — so this row reports Wikiquote’s account of it rather than a source we opened.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea is genuinely Galileo’s. The sentence is Martin’s, and on the page where it first appears it is not even in quotation marks ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Nineteenth-century France was busy deciding what the scientific method was, and Galileo was the figure it argued through. Cournot in 1847 and Martin in 1868 were both making the same case — that what separated Galileo from everyone before him was not experiment, which Bacon also urged, but measurement — and each wrote a summary sentence to carry it.

Martin’s summary was better than Cournot’s because he added the second half. Measuring what can be measured is only good practice; undertaking to make measurable the things that are not is a programme, and it is what actually happened over the following three centuries, from the thermometer to the questionnaire. A sentence that good does not stay a footnote in a French monograph. It gets promoted.
detailsBody: The promotion is visible in what happened to the two clauses. Cournot’s version, on p. 375 of his 1847 book on algebra and geometry ↗, is embedded in an argument about which parts of pure mathematics deserve to be called useful; it names Galileo but claims no words for him. Martin’s, twenty-one years later on p. 289 ↗, is a compact paraphrase in a chapter on method. Neither man was quoting. Somewhere between them and the modern slide deck the framing verb fell away, the quotation marks arrived, and the sentence acquired an author who had been dead for 226 years.

It is worth saying what this page is not claiming. Galileo really did insist on measurement, and really did build the instruments to do it — Martin’s own paragraph credits him with having “posé le principe” and invented the necessary instruments. The objection is narrower and it is about evidence: a sentence in quotation marks with a famous name under it is a claim about what a specific person wrote, and this one cannot be met. Martin was a Hellenist and historian of science ↗, and the words are his.
context.pull: Il déclare que… — three words that make the rest a summary, not a quotation.

German Wikiquote lists the line under "Zugeschrieben" and states that there is no evidence for it in Galileo’s writings, that the earliest mention is Thomas Henri Martin in 1868 with a shorter precursor from Antoine-Augustin Cournot in 1847, and that it was taken up and spread by Wilhelm Dilthey and Hermann Weyl, citing Kleinert 2009.

Page 289 of Th.-Henri Martin’s Galilée (Paris: Didier, 1868) reads "Il déclare que dans tous ces phénomènes il faut mesurer tout ce qui est mesurable, et tâcher de rendre mesurable tout ce qui ne l'est pas directement," in roman type, in indirect speech, with no quotation marks. Confirmed by reading the page image (running head GALILÉE, page number 289) and the OCR text.
The Internet Archive holds the complete 1868 scan of Martin’s Galilée : les droits de la science et la méthode des sciences physiques, published Paris: Didier.

Page 375 of Cournot’s De l'origine et des limites de la correspondance entre l'algèbre et la géométrie (Paris: L. Hachette, 1847) states that true physics was founded the day Galileo conceived the idea of assigning to experiments "pour objet immédiat la mesure de tout ce qui peut être mesurable dans les phénomènes naturels," with no second clause about making measurable what is not. Confirmed from the page image (running head CONSIDÉRATIONS GÉNÉRALES, page number 375).
The Internet Archive holds the complete 1847 scan of Cournot’s De l'origine et des limites de la correspondance entre l'algèbre et la géométrie, publisher L. Hachette.

French Wikipedia gives Thomas-Henri Martin’s dates as 4 February 1813 at Bellême to 9 February 1884 at Rennes, and describes him as a French Hellenist, historian of science and spiritualist philosopher, professor of ancient literature and dean of the Faculty of Letters at Rennes, who entered the École normale in 1831 and took a doctorate in 1836 with a Latin thesis on Spinoza.
English Wikipedia describes Antoine Augustin Cournot (1801–1877) as a French philosopher and mathematician who contributed to the development of economics.
